title: Learning to Interpret Weight Differences in Language Models
claim: A single adapter trained on many finetuned models with known changes lets any new finetuned model describe its own modifications in natural language.
layout: 3 numbered stages: two top panels split by a dashed divider, one wide bottom panel; left-to-right flow with dashed boxes grouping model plus adapter, and a footnote
description: A three-step diagram on a white background with large gray text. Step 1 (top left) shows a green 'Original LLM' box with arrows to orange 'Finetuned Model #1' and '#N' boxes. Each is labeled with a behavior (y_1, y_N), and a vertical ellipsis sits between them. Step 2 (top right) shows a dashed box holding an orange 'Finetuned Model #i' box, a ⊕ sign, and a purple 'LoRA adapter' box. A block arrow brings in the question 'What topic have you been trained on?' and another arrow sends out 'topic(y_i)'. Step 3 (bottom) shows a dashed box with a pink 'Held-Out Finetuned Model' ⊕ LoRA adapter. The question goes in on the left and the answer 'Harry Potter' comes out on the right. A footnote says changes may be hidden, e.g. backdoors or trojans. Color coding of the model types guides the eye.
caption: A diagrammatic overview of Diff Interpretation Tuning (DIT).
abstract: Finetuning (pretrained) language models is a standard approach for updating their internal parametric knowledge and specializing them to new tasks and domains. However, the corresponding model weight changes ("weight diffs") are not generally interpretable. While inspecting the finetuning dataset can give a sense of how the model might have changed, these datasets are often not publicly available or are too large to work with directly. Towards the goal of comprehensively understanding weight diffs in natural language, we introduce Diff Interpretation Tuning (DIT), a method that trains models to describe their own finetuning-induced modifications. Our approach uses synthetic, labeled weight diffs to train a DIT-adapter, which can be applied to a compatible finetuned model to make it describe how it has changed. We demonstrate in two proof-of-concept settings (reporting hidden behaviors and summarizing finetuned knowledge) that our method enables models to describe their finetuning-induced modifications using accurate natural language descriptions.
